model.label: Single-payer National Health Insurance run by a government agency, funded mainly by income-related premiums paid by the insured, employers and the government

overview.statement: When the NHI began in 1995, it merged the three main occupational insurance schemes, for workers, farmers and government employees, which together had covered roughly 59% of the population.
The NHI is now a single-payer insurance scheme run by the government, with the Ministry of Health and Welfare as the responsible authority.
Enrolment in the NHI is compulsory for every Republic of China national who has held a registered household in Taiwan for at least six months, and for every baby born in Taiwan.

locator.section: Ch. 2 Universal Healthcare Coverage, Equal Access to Medical Care

overview.statement: The NHI now also covers new immigrants, long-term foreign residents, overseas compatriot and foreign students and military personnel, and the second-generation NHI added prison inmates; foreigners qualify once they hold a resident certificate and have lived in Taiwan for six months in a row.

locator.section: Ch. 2 Universal Healthcare Coverage, Equal Access to Medical Care

overview.statement: At the end of December 2024 the NHI had 23,959,972 insured people.

locator.section: Ch. 2 Universal Healthcare Coverage, Equal Access to Medical Care

overview.statement: The Ministry of Health and Welfare reports that 23.88 million people were insured at the end of 2023, a coverage rate of 99.9%.

locator.section: Ch. 8, Section 1 Current Status of National Health Insurance

overview.statement: Local governments play little or no part in paying for care, and most NHI services are delivered by private providers, although some municipal governments own and run hospitals.
The Medical Care Act does not allow for-profit hospitals; most large private hospitals belong to foundations, and some small private ones are owned by individual doctors or groups of doctors.

financing.statement: NHI income comes mainly from premiums paid by the insured, employers and the government, with small additional amounts from late-payment charges, the Public Welfare Lottery surplus and the health and welfare surcharge on tobacco.

locator.section: Ch. 2 Balanced Finances and Sustainable Operations

financing.statement: Starting 1 January 2021, the NHI raised its general premium rate to 5.17% and its supplementary rate to 2.11%.
For the insured in categories 1 to 3 the premium is their premium-rated wage times the general rate; for categories 4 to 6 it is based on the average premium paid in categories 1 to 3.

The premium is split by fixed shares: for private- and public-sector employees the insured pays 30%, the employer 60% and the government 10%; for civil servants 30% and 70% by the employer; employers, the self-employed and independent professionals pay 100% themselves; occupational union members pay 60% and the government 40%; and farmers and fishermen pay 30% and the government 70%.
An insured person's premium counts at most three dependents, however many there are; the average number of dependents used in premium formulas has been 0.56 since 1 January 2024.
The government pays the whole premium for insured people in categories 4 and 5; from 1 January 2025 this average premium rose to NT$2,237 from NT$2,160.

For the insured in categories 1 to 3, premium-rated wages come from a payroll-bracket table set by the Ministry and approved by the Executive Yuan; the table in force since 1 January 2025 has 59 brackets.

locator.section: Ch. 2 Set Payroll Brackets for Calculating Premiums

financing.statement: A supplementary premium is also charged on six kinds of income that were previously left out of premium calculations: large bonuses, part-time pay, professional fees, dividends, interest and rent.

Members of low-income households do not pay supplementary premiums, and employers pay a supplementary premium on the difference between the wages they actually pay each month and the premium-rated wages declared for their staff.
Supplementary premiums raised about NT$71.5 billion in 2024, which was 8.9% of all NHI premium income that year.

Each year a committee made up of representatives of the insured, employers, providers, experts, independent members and government agencies, reviews the premium rate against the negotiated total of benefit payments; the result goes to the Ministry and then to the Executive Yuan for approval.

locator.section: Ch. 2 Balanced Finances and Sustainable Operations

financing.statement: Raising the premium rate above 6% requires the legislature to amend the NHI Act.
NHI revenue in 2024 was NT$834.4 billion and spending NT$811.0 billion, leaving a surplus of NT$23.4 billion and a cumulative balance of NT$162.2 billion.

locator.table: Table 2-6 NHI Revenues and Expenditures of the Past Five Years, row 2024

financing.statement: Central and local governments paid NT$36.17 billion in premium subsidies for 4.012 million people in disadvantaged groups in 2024, including low- and middle-to-low-income households, unemployed workers, people with disabilities and some Indigenous citizens.

locator.section: Ch. 6 Premium Subsidies for Underprivileged Groups

financing.statement: In Taiwan's 2024 health accounts, which classify spending by financing agent (who pays the provider), the NHI paid for 43.2% of national health expenditure, households 37.2% and government agencies 14.0%.
Household spending in these accounts excludes NHI premiums, because premiums are counted as NHI revenue and the care they pay for is already recorded under the NHI.
Because patients in Taiwan pay first and claim from private insurers afterwards, the official out-of-pocket figure also includes amounts that commercial insurance later reimburses.

locator.table: Table 10 Private Current Health Expenditure as % of Current Health Expenditure, note

financing.statement: The itemized income-tax deduction for insurance premiums has a NT$24,000 limit; the legislature has exempted labour, farmers', national pension and military, civil service and teacher insurance premiums from that limit, which the Ministry of Finance describes as mostly compulsory social insurance similar in nature to NHI premiums.

covered.statement: The NHI covers outpatient and inpatient care, traditional Chinese medicine, dental care, childbirth, rehabilitation, home care and chronic psychiatric rehabilitation, paying for diagnosis, tests, surgery, anaesthesia, drugs, devices, therapy, nursing and standard ward beds.
The NHI does not pay for glasses or equipment such as wheelchairs and hearing aids, but it does pay for cochlear implants for children.

locator.section: Services Covered by Public Health Insurance

covered.statement: At the end of 2024, 22,352 hospitals and clinics (91.01% of all those in Taiwan) had NHI contracts, alongside 7,649 contracted pharmacies, and the insured may choose freely among contracted providers.

Insured people who have an emergency illness or injury, or give birth, abroad and need immediate care can claim reimbursement within six months, up to the average paid to contracted providers in Taiwan in the previous quarter.
Through a dedicated fund, the NHI pays for every medicine the Ministry designates as necessary to treat a recognised rare disease.

locator.section: Ch. 6 Easing Copayment Burden on Specific Patients

covered.statement: Next-generation genetic sequencing is covered for 12 types of cancer, expected to benefit over 20,000 patients a year at a cost of about NT$300 million to the NHI budget.

locator.section: Ch. 5 NHI Coverage Policy for NGS Testing

covered.statement: Mental health care is covered both as outpatient care, including day care, and as inpatient care for acute and chronic conditions.

cost_sharing.statement: The basic outpatient copayment is NT$50 at clinics; at hospitals it depends on the level of hospital and whether the patient has a referral: NT$50 or NT$80 at district hospitals, NT$100 or NT$240 at regional hospitals and NT$170 or NT$420 at medical centres (with or without a referral). Dental and traditional Chinese medicine visits cost NT$50 at any level.

locator.table: Table 3-3 NHI Copayments for Outpatient Visits and Emergencies

cost_sharing.statement: Emergency visits cost NT$150 at clinics and district hospitals, NT$400 at regional hospitals and NT$750 at medical centres; low-income and near-poor households and people with disabilities pay NT$300 at regional hospitals and NT$550 at medical centres.

locator.table: Table 3-3 NHI Copayments for Outpatient Visits and Emergencies

cost_sharing.statement: No copayment is charged for care of a major illness or injury, for childbirth, for care in mountain areas or on offshore islands, or in certain other cases set by the NHIA.

locator.section: Ch. 3 Copayment and the User-Pays Principle

cost_sharing.statement: Inpatients pay between 5% and 30% of the cost, rising with the length of stay and different for acute and chronic beds; in 2025 the copayment was capped at NT$51,000 per stay for the same condition and NT$86,000 a year.

locator.table: Table 3-5 Copayment Rates for Inpatient Care

cost_sharing.statement: In areas lacking medical resources, copayments are cut by 20% and the home care copayment rate is halved from 10% to 5%.

locator.section: Ch. 3 Copayment and the User-Pays Principle

cost_sharing.statement: People with a disability certificate pay only the clinic-level outpatient copayment, whatever level of hospital or clinic they use.

locator.section: Ch. 6 Easing Copayment Burden on Specific Patients

cost_sharing.statement: Copayments are waived for treatment of 30 recognised catastrophic illnesses and injuries, such as cancer, chronic mental illness, dialysis and congenital disorders; at the end of 2024 more than 997,000 people (about 4.2% of the insured) held a valid certificate.

locator.section: Ch. 6 Persons with catastrophic illnesses and injuries

financial_hardship.statement: Since 7 June 2016 a person's NHI card is no longer blocked because of unpaid premiums or fees, so arrears do not cut off access to covered care once a person is enrolled.

locator.section: Ch. 6 Protecting the Right to Healthcare of the Underprivileged

financial_hardship.statement: Since 2018 the NHIA has used Article 37 of the NHI Act against long-term overseas residents and people who could pay but owe premiums; they are first sent a notice.

locator.section: Ch. 6 Protecting the Right to Healthcare of the Underprivileged

financial_hardship.statement: Only those who still have not paid their arrears after being notified have their cards suspended.

locator.section: Ch. 6 Protecting the Right to Healthcare of the Underprivileged

financial_hardship.statement: The NHIA lends interest-free to people in financial difficulty so they can pay premiums and unpaid copayments: NT$129 million across 1,276 cases in 2024, down from NT$152 million across 1,598 cases in 2023.
People who owe more than NT$2,000 in premiums and cannot repay at once can pay in instalments; such plans covered NT$2.226 billion in nearly 71,000 cases in 2024.
From 2008 to the end of 2024, Public Welfare Lottery money paid NT$5.220 billion to help 271,828 disadvantaged people with NHI premiums and fees.

locator.section: Ch. 6 Seeking for Public Welfare Lottery Contributions

financial_hardship.statement: A 2024 study found that out-of-pocket spending, including its two largest categories (curative care, and medical goods and medicines), fell disproportionately on people in poor health.

additional_care.statement: Almost 70% of people in Taiwan hold some private health insurance on top of the NHI; some plans pay for services the NHI excludes, but most mainly help with copayments and other cost sharing for covered care.
Private plans vary widely, with benefit amounts differing by as much as twentyfold, and the authors say this variation has left the public widely confused.

Private cover is sold by for-profit insurers, often with life or car insurance; it does not duplicate NHI services or buy faster access or more choice of specialists, but pays cash for specific diseases that can be spent on private rooms or devices the NHI does not cover, such as drug-eluting stents.

locator.section: The Role of Private Health Insurance

additional_care.statement: For medical devices that patients partly pay for themselves, the NHIA runs a platform where the public can compare the out-of-pocket price differences charged by different providers.

access.statement: In 2024 people made an average of 16.4 outpatient visits each; there were 14.8 hospital admissions per 100 people and 1.33 inpatient days per person.
Patients can go directly to any level of care without a referral, but copayments are set to steer them to lower-level providers first.

At the end of 2024, 522 community healthcare groups were operating, with 5,544 primary care clinics and 7,949 physicians (participation rates of 51.6% and 44.7%) and more than six million people benefiting.

locator.section: Ch. 3 Grand Family Physician Integrated Care System

access.statement: Taiwan had 270 practising physicians per 100,000 people in 2024, 29% more than in 2014.
In 2024 there were 626 registered nurses and 729 hospital beds per 100,000 people.

Since November 1999 the Integrated Delivery System has encouraged large hospitals to provide specialist, emergency and evening care in mountain and offshore-island areas; 50 townships and districts are designated, with 26 contracted institutions running 30 projects.

locator.section: Ch. 6 NHI Integrated Delivery System for mountain areas and offshore islands

access.statement: Specialist outpatient remote consultations numbered 12,651 in 2024, and emergency remote consultations 3,050.

outcomes.statement: Life expectancy at birth was 80.2 years in 2023, up 0.4 years on 2022 and 0.2 years above its 2013 level.
Life expectancy had risen for ten years until 2021 and then fell for two years in a row, mainly because of COVID-19.

In 2023, 18% of the population was 65 or older. The profile also reports that chronic non-communicable diseases cause 80% of deaths, that 92.4% of older adults have at least one chronic disease, and that healthy life expectancy at 65 is only 7.6 years.
Maternal mortality was 14 deaths per 100,000 live births in 2021, against 48 for the Western Pacific region.

locator.section: Quality and Outcomes: By the numbers

outcomes.statement: Infant mortality was 4.3 per 1,000 live births in 2023, slightly above the 4.1 the profile gives for high-income countries.

locator.section: Quality and Outcomes: By the numbers

costs.statement: National health expenditure was NT$1.8897 trillion in 2024, 3.0% more than in 2023; because nominal GDP grew 9.1%, it fell to 7.3% of GDP, or NT$80,719 per person.
The negotiated growth of the overall NHI global budget ranged from 3.32% to 5.64% a year between 2016 and 2025; it was 4.70% for 2024 and 5.50% for 2025.

locator.table: Table 3-6 Annual Negotiated Growth Rate of Global Budget, row Overall

costs.statement: Care for catastrophic illnesses and injuries cost more than NT$262.9 billion in 2024, 28.4% of all NHI medical spending, and about NT$90.3 billion (nearly 35%) of NHI drug spending goes to these conditions each year.

locator.section: Ch. 6 Persons with catastrophic illnesses and injuries

costs.statement: Long-term care spending was NT$223.9 billion in 2024; the public sector paid 45.4% of it, a share 27.9 percentage points higher than in 2014, and the private sector 54.6%.
Since a trial began on 1 January 2013, a drug expenditure target sets an annual drug budget; when spending exceeds it, an annual drug price adjustment is triggered automatically.

what_works.statement: The NHIA reports that public satisfaction with the NHI has stayed above 90% in each of the five years since 2020.
The Ministry credits the global budget payment system, introduced in 2002, with holding annual growth in medical spending to about 5%.

locator.section: Ch. 8, Section 4 Diverse Payment Methods and Rational Management

what_works.statement: Because the NHIA pays providers directly under one national fee schedule, physicians do not have to process claims for individual patients.
The My Health Bank personal health record service had about 11.91 million users from 2014 to the end of 2024, and about 90% of users said it helped them understand and monitor their health.

locator.section: Ch. 5 Value-Added Cloud Services: Application of My Health Bank

what_works.statement: The second-generation MediCloud system, launched in April 2024, brings together 13 categories of patients' records from different institutions, including medicines, imaging and other tests, surgery, discharge summaries, allergies and vaccinations.
In 2024 the remote-area delivery programmes served more than 480,000 residents of mountain and offshore-island townships, with average resident satisfaction of 96%.

locator.section: Ch. 6 NHI Integrated Delivery System for mountain areas and offshore islands

what_works.statement: A 2026 review of Taiwan's health technology assessment system reports that parallel review sped up access to new medicines without weakening the rigour of assessment.
Counselling for people with more than 90 outpatient visits a year cut the visits of those flagged in 2022 by an average of 16.01% after guidance in 2023, saving about NT$386 million.

locator.section: Ch. 8, Section 4 Diverse Payment Methods and Rational Management

problems.statement: Social and demographic change has made NHI spending grow much faster than premium income.

locator.section: Ch. 2 Balanced Finances and Sustainable Operations

problems.statement: A 2025 commentary lists budget strain, dissatisfaction among practitioners and coverage decisions that have blocked some new medicines and therapies among the challenges the NHI has faced.
The Commonwealth Fund profile reports that the fixed global budget has led to underinvestment in long-term health outcomes because it does not adjust for changing needs or new technology.
Because hospital budgets are fixed while each service is paid in points whose value floats, hospitals competed by raising volume, which pushed the value of a point below NT$1.
The same budget design controls costs efficiently from an administrative point of view but pushes institutions to maximise volume to stay financially stable.
In a survey of 59 hospitals after the Lunar New Year holiday, 41 (69.5%) reported abnormal emergency department operations such as severe overcrowding and difficulty admitting patients.
Longer waits for an inpatient bed in that survey were linked to fewer emergency department nurses and to closed general ward and intensive care beds.
Only about 60% of licensed nurses were working as nurses in 2023, and retention problems contribute to workforce challenges.
Life expectancy in Taitung County was 76.5 years in 2022, more than seven years below Taipei's 83.8 years.
Indigenous people had a life expectancy of 73.9 years in 2021, almost seven years below the national average.

Telemedicine was used more by people with higher incomes and with chronic or severe illness, which the authors read as a sign that poorer people in worse health were most likely to have unmet need for it.
The study's authors conclude that the NHI may not be meeting the care needs of people in poor health, who face a disproportionately high out-of-pocket burden.

reforms.statement: On 21 August 2026 the Legislative Yuan passed amendments to Articles 17 and 126 of the Income Tax Act, which change the itemized deduction for insurance premiums from tax year 2026 (returns filed in May 2027) once promulgated.

After a 2022 Constitutional Court ruling raised concerns about how NHI data are used, the legislature passed a National Health Insurance Data Management Statute in December 2025 to govern privacy and security of NHI data.

locator.section: Ch. 8 Refining Data Governance Mechanisms for NHI Sustainability

reforms.statement: From 1 January 2025 the government put NT$5 billion from its budget into the NHI fund for cancer drugs, and rules for provisional payment of new cancer drugs were issued on 25 February 2025.

locator.section: Ch. 5 Implementing the Provisional Payment System for New (Cancer) Drugs

reforms.statement: By June 2025, 11 new drugs and 5 coverage expansions had been listed under provisional payment, for conditions including lung, breast and colorectal cancer and multiple myeloma, and for cell therapies such as CAR-T.

locator.section: Ch. 5 Implementing the Provisional Payment System for New (Cancer) Drugs

reforms.statement: In 2024 the government ended the option for nationals living abroad to suspend NHI cover and resume it on return; they must now keep paying premiums wherever they live or leave the system altogether.
Since 1 January 2024 a drug company can apply for NHI reimbursement at the same time as for a marketing licence, and the listing should take effect within six months of the licence.
Next-generation sequencing tests were added to NHI coverage on 1 May 2024.

locator.section: Ch. 5 NHI Coverage Policy for NGS Testing

reforms.statement: In July 2023 copayments for outpatient medicines and emergency care were raised, with higher limits at medical centres and regional hospitals, while primary care clinics, low- and middle-income people and people with disabilities were left unchanged.

locator.section: Ch. 3 Copayment and the User-Pays Principle

reforms.statement: The Ministry is carrying out a Nursing Workforce Preparation Plan for 2023-2030, with 12 strategies across ministries to address the nursing shortage and improve working conditions.
Besides widening the revenue base and saving costs, the NHIA has raised the premium rate three times, in 2002, 2010 and 2021.

locator.section: Ch. 2 Balanced Finances and Sustainable Operations

reforms.statement: The second-generation NHI of January 2013 improved finances further by widening the income base through supplementary premiums and higher government contributions.

locator.section: Ch. 2 Balance of NHI Revenues and Expenditures

us_lessons.statement: A 2025 commentary argues that, given their scope, both US Medicare and Taiwan's NHI face budget pressures that lead to policies leaving coverage gaps, and that private insurance has emerged in both countries to fill them.
The commentary points to the standardisation of US Medigap plans into lettered types as a model Taiwan could use to reduce confusion over its varied private plans.
The same authors caution that the Medicare program it draws on is itself burdened by complexity and high cost.

The authors of a 2026 review of Taiwan's health technology assessment system conclude that its experience can guide other health systems trying to balance access to new technology, evidence building and financial sustainability.
